abstract: Optically Pumped Magnetometer magnetoencephalography (OP-MEG) enables flexible, close-to-scalp recordings unlocking access to new patient cohorts and naturalistic paradigms. The data collected during OP-MEG sessions is naturally multi-dimensional, often containing information across patients, trials, conditions, space, frequency and time which can be stored in tensors. Canonical polyadic decomposition (CPD) is an unsupervised method that separates multidimensional data into components with linked spatial, spectral and temporal profiles. This allows neural responses to be characterised across brain regions, frequency and time simultaneously,without specifying these features in advance. This makes CPD well suited to OP-MEG data, where signals naturally vary across these dimensions. Here, we applied CPD to whole-brain, source-reconstructed OP-MEG data from three participants with epilepsy during a simple visuomotor task, modelling neural activity jointly across brain regions, frequency and time. We split these subject-specific tensors into event-related power decrease and increase (referred to as ERD and ERS for convenience) tensors so that a more interpretable and computationally efficient non-negative CPD variant could be applied. CPD paired with consensus clustering on spatio-spectral-temporal networks successfully identified cross-patient, simultaneous motor beta and visual alpha suppression. Permutation-based null distribution tests were used to exclude tensors that lacked significant low-rank structure. These findings demonstrate the applicability of tensor decompositions to electrophysiological data as the pipeline recovers canonical visuomotor responses without prespecifying region, band or latency.
